content: Infants in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) are exposed to a highly stressful environment characterized by continuous, high-intensity noise and bright light. Additionally, they lack the tactile stimulation they would typically receive in the womb or through general maternal care. Massage has been proposed as a potential intervention to address these issues, as it may reduce stress and provide tactile stimulation, potentially promoting growth and development in preterm and low-birth-weight infants. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether preterm and/or low-birth-weight infants who receive massage therapy experience improved weight gain and earlier hospital discharge compared to those receiving standard care. Additionally, the study aimed to assess whether massage has any other beneficial or harmful effects on this population. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's specialized register, the Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Psychlit, CINAHL, and Dissertation Abstracts International, up to July 1, 2003. Additional references were identified through citation tracking, personal files, and correspondence with experts. There were no restrictions on language. The inclusion criteria were randomized trials involving infants born at less than 37 weeks of gestation or weighing less than 2500 grams at birth, who received systematic tactile stimulation via human hands. At least one outcome related to weight gain, length of hospital stay, behavior, or development had to be reported. Data were extracted independently by three reviewers and included baseline characteristics of the sample, weight gain, length of stay, and behavioral and developmental outcomes. Physiological and biochemical outcomes were not recorded. Statistical analysis followed standard Cochrane Collaboration methods. The results showed that massage interventions improved daily weight gain by an average of 5.1 grams (95% confidence interval [CI]: 3.5 to 6.7 grams). However, gentle, still touch did not demonstrate any significant benefit, with an increase in daily weight gain of only 0.2 grams (95% CI: -1.2 to 1.6 grams). Massage interventions also appeared to reduce the length of hospital stay by an average of 4.5 days (95% CI: 2.4 to 6.5 days), although there were concerns about the methodological rigor, particularly regarding the blinding of this outcome. There was some evidence suggesting a slight positive effect of massage on postnatal complications and weight at 4 to 6 months of age. However, serious concerns about the methodological quality of the included studies, especially regarding selective reporting of outcomes, undermine the reliability of these findings. The authors concluded that the evidence supporting the benefits of massage for developmental outcomes in preterm infants is weak and does not justify widespread implementation of massage therapy for this population. In settings where nurses currently provide massage, it is important to consider whether this represents a cost-effective use of their time. Future research should focus on evaluating the effects of massage interventions on clinical outcomes, such as medical complications and length of hospital stay, as well as process-of-care outcomes, including caregiver or parental satisfaction.
